title: Big-O complexity
examples: What does O(n) mean for an algorithm?
How do I know if my code is O(n^2)?
Is O(log n) always better than O(n)?

explain.say: Today we look at how fast algorithms run.
Constant time, or O of one, is the best.
Linear time, or O of n, means time grows with input size.
Quadratic time, or O of n squared, grows very fast.
Logarithmic time, or O of log n, is very efficient.
Imagine searching a sorted dictionary for a word.

faq.q: What does Big-O notation actually measure?
faq.a: It describes the rate at which the running time increases as the input size grows. It focuses on the upper bound of time.
asks: How do I measure algorithm speed?
What does the 'O' stand for in this context?

faq.q: Is O(n) always slower than O(log n)?
faq.a: Yes, for large enough inputs, a lower order of growth means it is more efficient. Logarithmic growth is much slower than linear growth.
asks: Which is better, n or log n?
Does the input size matter for comparison?

faq.q: How do I find the complexity if I have nested loops?
faq.a: Nested loops often result in multiplication of complexities. Two nested loops of size n give O(n squared).
asks: If I have two loops, what do I do?
What is the complexity of nested iteration?

faq.q: Does O(1) mean the code runs instantly?
faq.a: No, it means the time taken does not depend on the input size. It is constant time regardless of how big the input is.

faq.q: What is the difference between O(n) and O(n log n)?
faq.a: O(n log n) is generally better than O(n) because the log factor reduces the overall growth rate significantly for large inputs.
asks: Which is faster: n or n log n?
Can you compare these two growth rates?

facts: O(1) means the time taken is constant, no matter the input size.
O(n) means the time taken grows directly proportional to the input size.
O(n²) occurs when you have nested loops iterating over the same input.
O(log n) typically occurs when you repeatedly halve the problem size.

quiz.say: If an algorithm processes every item in a list exactly once, what is its time complexity?
quiz.why: Processing every item once means the time scales directly with the number of items, which is linear.

wrong.1: This would mean the time taken never changes, even if the list gets longer.
wrong.2: This suggests the problem size is being halved each time, which is not what happens when processing every item.
wrong.3: This implies that for every item, you are checking every other item, which is more work than just processing once.

quiz.say: Which complexity describes an operation like accessing an element in an array by its index?
quiz.why: Accessing an element by its known position takes the same amount of time regardless of the array's size.

wrong.0: This would mean you are comparing every element against every other element.
wrong.2: This suggests you have to check every element to find the one you want.
wrong.3: This implies you are repeatedly halving the search space, which is not necessary for direct access.

quiz.say: If an algorithm repeatedly divides the problem size in half, like in binary search, what is the complexity?
quiz.why: Halving the problem size at each step leads to logarithmic time complexity, which is very efficient.

wrong.0: This would mean you are checking every single element sequentially.
wrong.1: This suggests the time taken is constant, which is not true as the input size decreases.
wrong.2: This suggests the work increases quadratically, which is much slower than halving the problem.
